In this lesson, you will learn about the make up of a microwave receiver.
INTRODUCTIONM
Recall that the purpose of a microwave communication system is to:
Process, Transmit, Receive and Interface information to the user.
The receiver section contains an antenna system, waveguide system, receiver and information processor.
The circuits used can be completely different from one receiver to the next.
Let's begin the lesson on MICROWAVE RECEIVERS.............................

MICROWAVE RECEIVERS
This is a block diagram of a typical microwave receiver....
DISCUSSION
At first glance, it may appear that it does not contain all the necessary stages that a receiver must have.
But it does! Let's cover each stage, starting with the Antenna.
The antenna picks up transmitted microwave signals and funnels them to the waveguide system.
They direct the microwave RF energy into the receiver.
The receiver is comprised of many components.
The down converter changes the carrier frequency to the IF frequency.
The IF frequency is lower than the carrier frequency so waveguides are not needed beyond this point. Coaxial cables can be used now instead.
The down converter consists of an RF amplifier, local oscillator and mixer.
The modulated IF frequency is routed to a high gain amplifier to boost the signal to a usable level.
After amplification, the IF signal is sent to the FM discriminator to remove the information from the carrier.
The AFT (automatic frequency tracking) circuit samples the IF signal from the high gain amplifier.
If the IF is not the correct frequency, the AFT circuit sends a DC signal back to the down converter to change the local oscillator frequency.
This action maintains the correct IF frequency even if the carrier frequency drifts.
The information processor in this basic receiver is an amplifier.
The 6 MHz band width allows for video and multiplex signals to be amplified.
A multiplexed information signal requires additional information processing to separate the messages.
Where is the IF frequency generated?
The FM discriminator removes information from the IF carrier signal.

The receiver circuit is located on PC130-308 in the Nida Model 330 Microwave Trainer.
IC7 is a +12 VDC voltage regulator. It receives +15 VDC.
The +12 VDC is routed to the down converter via J2 and is also used for power to IC4 and IC5 in the amplifier and AFT circuits.
IC6 is a +6 VDC voltage regulator. It also receives +15 VDC.
+6 VDC is used for IC1 and IC2 in the high gain amplifier. It is also used by IC3 in the AFT circuit.
IC8 is a -6 VDC voltage regulator. It receives -15 VDC.
-6 VDC is used for IC1 and IC2 in the high gain amplifier. It is also used by IC3 in the AFT circuit.
Test points are provided for monitoring the three voltages.
The high gain amplifier is made up of IC1 and IC2. The input is from the down converter via J1.
The IF input, (50 MHz is used in the Nida Model 330 Microwave Trainer) passes through a filter before being applied to the high gain amplifier.
The output of IC2 is rectified by D1 and applied to the IC3 in the FM discriminator, and to the AFT circuit, IC5.
TP3 is provided to monitor the rectified IF signal.
Also, R6 controls the amount of AGC, (Automatic Gain Control). TP1 is provided to monitor this DC voltage.
IC3 is the FM discriminator that reproduces the information. C15 is used to adjust it for proper operation.
IC3 operates in a phase lock mode that produces a signal that is proportional to the variations in the IF frequency.
IC5 and IC9 are the AFT circuit. It's input is from the high gain amplifier.
The circuit develops a DC voltage that controls the frequency of the local oscillator in the down converter.
The AFT signal is sent to the AFT/NML switch.
In the AFT position, the control voltage from IC5 maintains a LO frequency that produces an IF of 50 MHz.
In the NML (normal) position, +12 VDC is divided to produce a DC voltage that keeps the LO at 10.450 GHz.
If the IF carrier is 10.5 MHz the LO frequency will be kept at
R22, AFT ADJ, is used to adjust the AFT circuit for proper operation. TP5 is provided to monitor the AFT voltage.
L3 set the operation of the circuit. This adjustment is set and need not be changed.
IC4 is the 6 MHz bandwidth amplifier. R17 is the gain adjust. TP4 (input) and an Output test point are provided for monitoring these signals.
Remember, other microwave receivers may use different circuits. The circuits shown are typical receiver circuits.

1. A microwave communication system's purpose is to: Process, Transmit, Receive and Interface Information to the user.
2. A basic microwave receiver: Receives information, down converts the frequency, demodulates the signal and processes the information for the user.
3. The waveguide system includes the antenna, waveguide and down-converter.
4. The electronic circuitry includes a power supply, amplifier, AFT circuit and a FM discriminator.
5. The Nida microwave circuitry is contained on one PC card, PC130-308.
6. The high gain amplifier boosts the IF signal to a usable level. The 6 MHz bandwidth amplifier boosts the demodulated signal.
7. The FM discriminator removes the information from the IF signal. The AFT circuit maintains the down-converter output at 50 MHz.
8. The power supply applies +12, +6 and -6 VDC to the IC's. It also applies +12 VDC to the down-converter.
